questions.problem: Let $F(x,y,z)={y}^{2}\,i-{x}^{2}\,j+5\,k$ and let $C$ be a path in ${R}^{3}.$ Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r?$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field 

$$
F(x,y,z)=P(x,y,z)\,i+Q(x,y,z)\,j+R(x,y,z)\,k
$$

defined on $C,$ we have

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{C}P(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y+R(x,y,z)\,\text{d}z.
$$

Therefore, in our case, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x-{x}^{2}\,\text{d}y+5\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $C$ is the closed polygonal path $LMNL,$ shown in the diagram above, traversed in the counterclockwise direction?
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed in counterclockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

$$
C={C}_{1}\cup {-{C}_{2}}\cup {C}_{3},
$$

where $-{C}_{2}$ is the same path as ${C}_{2}$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14060128/assets/0e4a78829ce8d1135d46dda1db59c968c0306937d9c5a45b24fa41648a679ea4.png)

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a line segment from the point $O(0,0)$ to the point $A(2,0),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(2,0)$ to the point $B(1,1).$

Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=2,$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(x+y)\,i+(x-y)\,j,$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the first integral, so we only need to work out the second.

The path ${C}_{2}$ is the line segment from $A$ to $B.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =⟨2,0⟩+t(⟨1,1⟩-⟨2,0⟩) \\  & =⟨2-t,t⟩ \\  & =(2-t)\,i+t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<1.$ Along this segment, we have $x=2-t$ and $y=t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t)) & =(x+y)\,i+(x-y)\,j \\  & =(2-t+t)\,i+(2-t-t)\,j \\  & =2\,i+(2-2t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =-i+j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =(2\,i+(2-2t)\,j)\cdot (-i+j) \\  & =-2+(2-2t) \\  & =-2t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =2+{\int }_{0}^{1}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2+{\int }_{0}^{1}(-2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2-{t}^{2}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2-(1-0) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a the line segment from the point $A(-2,0)$ to the point $B(0,1),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of the line segment from the point $B(0,1)$ to the point $D(1,1).$

Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=-\frac{3}{2},$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(x-2y)\,i+(y-x)\,j,$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the second integral, so we only need to work out the first.

The path ${C}_{1}$ is the line segment from $A$ to $B.$  It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =⟨-2,0⟩+t(⟨0,1⟩-⟨-2,0⟩) \\  & =⟨-2+2t,t⟩ \\  & =(-2+2t)i+t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<1.$ Along this segment, we have $x=-2+2t$ and $y=t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t)) & =(x-2y)\,i+(y-x)\,j \\  & =((-2+2t)-2t)\,i+(t-(-2+2t))\,j \\  & =-2\,i+(2-t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2+2t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =2\,i+j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =(-2\,i+(2-t)\,j)\cdot (2\,i+j) \\  & =-2-t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t+(-\frac{3}{2}) \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-2-t)\,\text{d}t-\frac{3}{2} \\  & ={[-2t-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1}-\frac{3}{2} \\  & =[-2(1)-\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}-0]-\frac{3}{2} \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}-\frac{3}{2} \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a the line segment from the point $A(0,1)$ to the point $B(1,2),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a line segment from the point $B(1,2)$ to the point $D(1,3).$

Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=\frac{7}{2},$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(2x-3y)\,i+(x+y)\,j,$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the second integral, so we only need to work out the first.

The path ${C}_{1}$ is the line segment from $A$ to $B.$  It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =⟨0,1⟩+t(⟨1,2⟩-⟨0,1⟩) \\  & =⟨t,1+t⟩ \\  & =t\,i+(1+t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<1.$ Along this segment, we have $x=t$ and $y=1+t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t)) & =(2x-3y)\,i+(x+y)\,j \\  & =(2t-3(1+t))\,i+(t+(1+t))\,j \\  & =(-3-t)\,i+(2t+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =((-3-t)\,i+(2t+1)\,j)\cdot (i+j) \\  & =-3-t+2t+1 \\  & =t-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t+\frac{7}{2} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t-2)\,\text{d}t+\frac{7}{2} \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}-2t]}_{0}^{1}+\frac{7}{2} \\  & =[\frac{1}{2}-2-0]+\frac{7}{2} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}+\frac{7}{2} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(1,-1)$ to the point $B(1,1),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a line segment from the point $B(1,1)$ to the point $O(0,0).$

Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=2,$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(2x+y)\,i+(x-2y)\,j,$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the first integral, so we only need to work out the second.

The path ${C}_{2}$ is the line segment from $B$ to $O.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}(t) & =b+t(0-b) \\  & =⟨1,1⟩+t(⟨0,0⟩-⟨1,1⟩) \\  & =⟨1-t,1-t⟩ \\  & =(1-t)\,i+(1-t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<1.$ Along this segment, we have $x=1-t$ and $y=1-t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t)) & =(2x+y)\,i+(x-2y)\,j \\  & =(2(1-t)+(1-t))\,i+((1-t)-2(1-t))\,j \\  & =(3-3t)\,i+(-1+t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)j \\  & =-i-j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =((3-3t)\,i+(-1+t)\,j)\cdot (-i-j) \\  & =-3+3t+1-t \\  & =-2+2t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =2+{\int }_{0}^{1}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2+{\int }_{0}^{1}(-2+2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2+(-2t+{t}^{2})\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2+(1-2) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

$$

We're given the value of the second integral, so we only need to work out the first.

${C}_{1}$ is the section of parabola $y={x}^{2}$ from $O$ to $A.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}(t)=t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<2.$ Along this curve, we have $x=t$ and $y={t}^{2}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t)) & =x\,i+y\,j \\  & =t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})j \\  & =i+2t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =(t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j)\cdot (i+2t\,j) \\  & =t+2{t}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t-2 \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(t+2{t}^{3})\,\text{d}t-2 \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{t}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{2}-2 \\  & =[2+8]-2 \\  & =10-2 \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Establishing the Connection With Line Integrals of Scalar Fields
canonical_examples.problem: Let $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = (3x+2) \: \mathbf{i} - y^3 \: \mathbf{j}$ and let $C$ be a path in $\mathbb R^2.$ Write $\displaystyle \int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}$ in the form $\displaystyle\int_C P(x,y)\,\textrm d x +  Q(x,y)\,\textrm d y.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field 

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y) = P(x,y) \: \mathbf{i} + Q(x,y) \: \mathbf{j}
$$

defined on $C,$ we have

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} = \int\limits_C P(x,y) \: \text{d}x + Q(x,y) \: \text{d}y.
$$

In our case, $P = 3x+2$ and $Q = -y^3.$ Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}(3x+2)\,\text{d}x-{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Using the Properties of Line Integrals of Vector-Valued Functions
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14060128/assets/38ab4af726729b5c9804f4aa13801d637e5e62eda085d6611174586827ef8c11.png)

Consider the integral $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $C$ is the closed polygonal path $FGHF$ shown above, traversed in the **clockwise** direction. Express this integral as a sum of line integrals along $C_1, C_2,$ and $C_3.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed in clockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

$$
C = \{-C_1\} \cup \{-C_2\} \cup C_3,
$$

where $-C_1$ and $-C_2$ are the same paths as $C_1$ and $C_2$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{-{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Line Integral of a Vector-Valued Function Along a Union of Curves
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14060128/assets/001487e4a94988a24d15702a18692e9deb2495a7cc7ec5c9f71b98fea13e0ce8.png)

The path $C_1$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(-2,0)$ to the point $O(0,0),$ and the path $C_2$ consists of a line segment from the point $O(0,0)$ to the point $B(1,1).$

Given that $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = -4,$ evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf{F}(x, y) = (2x-3y) \,\mathbf{i} + (2y-5x)\,\mathbf {j}$ and $C = C_1\cup C_2.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
\int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r}
+
 \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r}.
$$

We're given the value of the first integral, so we only need to work out the second.

The path $C_2$ is the line segment from $O$ to $B.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}(t) & =b+t(c-b) \\  & =⟨0,0⟩+t(⟨1,1⟩-⟨0,0⟩) \\  & =⟨t,t⟩ \\  & =t\,i+t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0 \lt t \lt 1.$ Along this segment, we have $x = t$ and $y = t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t)) & =(2x-3y)\,i+(2y-5x)\,j \\  & =(2t-3t)\,i+(2t-5t)\,j \\  & =-t\,i-3t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =(-t\,i-3t\,j)\cdot (i+j) \\  & =-t\cdot 1+(-3t)\cdot 1 \\  & =-4t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-4+{\int }_{0}^{1}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4+{\int }_{0}^{1}(-4t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4+[-2{t}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =-4+[-2+0] \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$
